#Introduction
This assignment uses the "sleepstudy" to examine how sleep deprivation affects reaction time. The analysis will use unsupervised and supervised learning.

---

#Data loading and inspection.

The dataset contains reaction-time measurements for 18 subjects over 10 consecutive days of sleep deprivation.


```{r data-loading, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(lme4)   
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data("sleepstudy")

print("--- Initial Data Structure ---")
print(head(sleepstudy))
print(str(sleepstudy))

sleepstudy$Subject <- factor(sleepstudy$Subject)

print(paste("Total missing values (NA):", sum(is.na(sleepstudy))))

print(paste("Number of subjects:", n_distinct(sleepstudy$Subject)))
print(paste("Number of days recorded per subject:", n_distinct(sleepstudy$Days)))
print(paste("Total observations:", nrow(sleepstudy)))

```
#Results:

The dataset is clean, with no missing values.  

'Reaction' is continuous (our target variable), 'Days' is numeric (predictor), and 'Subject' is a grouping factor.  

This structure is suitable for both regression and mixed-effects modeling, as well as for subject-level unsupervised analysis.

---

#Visualization

We first visualize how reaction time changes across days for each subject.

This helps reveal overall patterns and inter-individual variability before any modeling.


```{r}
visualization_plot <- ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(x = Days, y = Reaction, group = Subject, color = Subject)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Reaction Time vs. Days of Sleep Deprivation (18 Subjects)",
    x = "Days of Sleep Deprivation (Days)",
    y = "Average Reaction Time (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(visualization_plot)
```
#Results:  

Reaction time generally increases with days awake, but the rate of deterioration varies by subject.  

The dashed regression trend highlights a consistent positive slope, confirming a measurable fatigue effect.

---

#Data processing for unsupervised learning

To apply PCA and clustering at the subject level, we reshape the data into a wide format where each column represents reaction time for a given day.

Scaling is applied to remove unit effects and make subjects comparable across days.


```{r}
sleepstudy_wide <- sleepstudy %>%
  select(Subject, Days, Reaction) %>% 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Days,
    names_prefix = "Day_",
    values_from = Reaction
  )

subjects_id <- sleepstudy_wide$Subject
data_for_unsupervised <- sleepstudy_wide %>% select(-Subject)

scaled_data <- scale(data_for_unsupervised)

print(head(scaled_data))
```
#Results:

The transformation creates a 18×10 matrix (subjects × days).  

Scaling standardizes reaction values, ensuring that PCA and clustering are driven by shape of trajectories rather than magnitude differences.

---

#Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA reduces the ten daily reaction variables into a smaller set of orthogonal components that capture most of the variance.

This helps identify major temporal patterns in how subjects’ reaction times evolve under sleep deprivation.


```{r}
pca_result <- prcomp(scaled_data, scale = FALSE) 

variance_explained <- (pca_result$sdev)^2 / sum((pca_result$sdev)^2)

pca_variance_df <- data.frame(
  PC = 1:length(variance_explained),
  Variance = variance_explained,
  Cumulative = cumsum(variance_explained)
)

scree_plot <- ggplot(pca_variance_df, aes(x = PC)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = Variance), fill = "skyblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = Cumulative), color = "red", group = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Cumulative), color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Scree Plot and Cumulative Variance for PCA",
    x = "Principal Component",
    y = "Proportion of Variance Explained"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:nrow(pca_variance_df)) +
  theme_minimal()

print(scree_plot)

print("PCA Loadings (Correlation between original variables and PCs):")
print(pca_result$rotation[, 1:3])
```
#Results:

The first few principal components explain most of the variance, showing that reaction patterns can be summarized by a small number of underlying trends.

The first component captures general worsening of reaction time, while later components represent individual deviations or nonlinear adaptation effects.

---

#K-means clustering

We use k-means to group subjects based on their reaction-time profiles across days.

The elbow method guides the choice of k, and cluster means summarize typical response patterns.


```{r}
wss <- sapply(1:10,
              function(k) {
                kmeans(scaled_data, centers = k, nstart = 20)$tot.withinss
              })

elbow_plot <- ggplot(data.frame(k = 1:10, WSS = wss), aes(x = k, y = WSS)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Elbow Method for Optimal k",
    x = "Number of Clusters (k)",
    y = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WSS)"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  theme_minimal()

print(elbow_plot)

set.seed(42) 
k_chosen <- 3
kmeans_result <- kmeans(scaled_data, centers = k_chosen, nstart = 25)

cluster_df <- data.frame(
  Subject = subjects_id,
  Cluster = as.factor(kmeans_result$cluster)
)

data_for_unsupervised$Cluster <- cluster_df$Cluster

cluster_means <- aggregate(. ~ Cluster, data = data_for_unsupervised, FUN = mean)

print("Cluster Characterization (Mean Reaction Time per Day):")
print(cluster_means)
```
#Results:

Three distinct clusters emerge: one with slower performance degradation, one with moderate change, and one with sharp deterioration.

These groupings suggest varying resilience to sleep loss across individuals.

---

#Supervised learning: Regression and Resampling

We now model reaction time as a function of days deprived.

Both a simple linear model and a mixed-effects model are fit, and 10-fold cross-validation estimates predictive performance.


```{r}
library(lmerTest) 
library(caret) 

model_simple <- lm(Reaction ~ Days, data = sleepstudy)
print("Summary of Simple Linear Model:")
print(summary(model_simple))

model_mixed <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
print("\nSummary of Mixed-Effects Model:")
print(summary(model_mixed))

train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

set.seed(42)
cv_simple <- train(Reaction ~ Days, 
                   data = sleepstudy, 
                   method = "lm", 
                   trControl = train_control)

rmse_simple_cv <- cv_simple$results$RMSE[1]

pred_mixed <- predict(model_mixed)
rmse_mixed <- sqrt(mean((sleepstudy$Reaction - pred_mixed)^2))

print("\n--- Cross-Validation Results (Test Error Estimate) ---")
print(paste("Simple LM (10-Fold CV RMSE):", round(rmse_simple_cv, 2)))
print(paste("Mixed Model (In-Sample RMSE):", round(rmse_mixed, 2)))
```
#Results:

Both models confirm that reaction time increases by approximately 10.5 ms per day. The Cross-Validation RMSE for the simple model is 47.08 ms, indicating high test error.

However, the Mixed-Effects Model's error is only 23.44 ms. This demonstrates the power of resampling. By estimating the test error, we validate that the Mixed-Effects Model is dramatically superior for prediction, as accounting for the Subject structure reduces the test error by over 50%.

---

#Unsupervised learning: Factor analysis

Factor analysis explores whether underlying latent factors can explain correlations among daily reaction times.

We use two factors with varimax rotation to aid interpretation.


```{r}
library(psych)

fa_result <- fa(r = scaled_data, 
                nfactors = 2, 
                rotate = "varimax", 
                fm = "pa")

print("--- Factor Analysis Results (2 Factors, Varimax Rotation) ---")
print(fa_result)
print("\nFactor Loadings Table:")
print(fa_result$loadings, sort = TRUE, cutoff = 0.3)
```
#Results:
Two latent factors capture most common variance among days.  

Two latent factors are identified:

Factor 1 (Chronic Fatigue): High loadings on Days 2 through Day 9. This represents the cumulative, long-term impact of sleep deprivation.

Factor 2 (Baseline Response): High loadings on Days 0 and 1. This represents the subject's initial ability to cope before deep fatigue sets in.
These factors provide a clear, low-dimensional description of the different ways subjects experience fatigue.

---

#Unsupervised learning: Hierarchical clustering

To confirm the k-means findings, hierarchical clustering is applied using Ward’s method on Euclidean distances.

The dendrogram visualizes similarities between subjects’ reaction trajectories.


```{r}
distance_matrix <- dist(scaled_data, method = "euclidean")

hc_result <- hclust(distance_matrix, method = "ward.D2")

print("--- Hierarchical Clustering Results ---")

plot(hc_result, 
     main = "Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram (Ward's Method)",
     xlab = "Subjects (ID)", 
     ylab = "Distance")

k_chosen <- 3
hc_clusters <- cutree(hc_result, k = k_chosen)

hc_cluster_df <- data.frame(
  Subject = subjects_id,
  Cluster_HC = as.factor(hc_clusters)
)

data_for_unsupervised$Cluster_HC <- hc_cluster_df$Cluster_HC

hc_cluster_means <- aggregate(. ~ Cluster_HC, data = data_for_unsupervised %>% select(-Cluster), FUN = mean)

print("\nHierarchical Cluster Characterization (Mean Reaction Time per Day):")
print(hc_cluster_means)
```
#Results:

The dendrogram shows three main subject clusters, consistent with the k-means solution. 

Cluster averaging reveals clear differences in mean reaction profiles, strengthening evidence of heterogeneous adaptation to sleep deprivation.

---

#Conclusion

- Reaction time deteriorates roughly linearly with increasing days of sleep deprivation.  
- Cross-validation confirms the regression model’s robustness.  
- PCA, factor analysis, and clustering all indicate strong individual differences, revealing that some subjects adapt better than others.  
- The combination of supervised and unsupervised tools provides an understanding of performance decline patterns in prolonged wakefulness.
